newsitem.title: SWEDEN: OECD says sees Sweden GDP two pct '97, 2.3 pct '98.
newsitem.headline: OECD says sees Sweden GDP two pct '97, 2.3 pct '98.

text.p: The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Thursday it expected Swedish Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to rise two percent in 1997 and 2.3 percent in 1998.
The Paris-based group said in its half-yearly report it saw the implicit price deflator at 1.9 percent in 1997 and 2.5 percent the following year.

It expected private consumption to rise 1.8 percent this year and by 2.1 percent in 1998. Unemployment, seen at 8.1 percent in 1997 and 7.5 percent in 1998, would continue to haunt the Swedish economy, it said.
The OECD said economic growth which began last year should continue as the government's effective fiscal measures to restore budget balance came to a close.
"The expansion should be supported by accelerating growth in domestic demand as monetary conditions remain favourable and the 1995-98 fiscal consolidation programme is coming to an end.

"Employment creation is likely to remain weak, since wage growth is only gradually adapting to high unemployment and the establishment of a low-inflation environment, thereby weakening the basis for sustained expansion of the business sector."

Despite negative employment growth since the second quarter of 1996, wage inflation remains strong but should decelerate in 1997. It said inflation has been capped by high productivity growth in manufacuturing and reduced profit margins.
The OECD said a few well-performing sectors should continue to bolster exports but the strengthening crown should gradually erode export market shares.

Households and domestically oriented industries will become more important in underpinning economic growth. "In this respect, the fall in interest rates and stronger income growth as the effect of the fiscal consolidation wears off will benefit private consumption and residential investment, in turn supporting business investment," it said.
The main downward risk is unemployment, which will be aggravated if the wage agreements which come up for renewal in 1998 are high, it said.
"In this case, labour-shedding would intensify, adversely affecting consumer spending and adding to the strain on fiscal policy following from low employment growth," it said.
